title: Beyond Sustainability, Design for Well-Being: Gaudí's Monument to Nature, Biomimetic Functions with Biophilic Morphology
central_proposition: Architects can create more sustainable, efficient, and human-centric buildings by combining biomimicry's functional principles with biophilia's visual-psychological qualities, as exemplified by Antoni Gaudí's Sagrada Família.

concept_definitions.name: Biomimicry
concept_definitions.definition: an architectural approach that encourages drawing inspiration of functions, concepts, and strategies from natural organisms or systems to improve the built environment and its capacity for regenerative systems

concept_definitions.name: Biophilia
concept_definitions.definition: the missing link in sustainable design to make the built environment more pleasing, enjoyable and healthy; human health and well-being has a biologically based need to affiliate with nature

concept_definitions.name: Optimum healthy environment
concept_definitions.definition: the conditions that tend to 'promote or permit the optimal physiological, mental, and social performance in its natural or 'evolutionary' environment'

concept_definitions.name: Block system structure
concept_definitions.definition: where each section, made up in turn of a series of elements, forms a block

concept_definitions.name: Modularity
concept_definitions.definition: joining together standardized units to form larger compositions

concept_definitions.name: Fractal
concept_definitions.definition: a pattern that repeats itself at different scales to an infinitely small scale

concept_definitions.name: Ruled surfaces
concept_definitions.definition: a set of points swept by a moving straight line

argument_structure: The paper introduces biomimicry and biophilia, highlighting their individual strengths and limitations. It then proposes a combined approach to address these limitations, using Antoni Gaudí's Sagrada Família as a pioneering example that implicitly integrated both functional biomimicry and visual-psychological biophilia. The argument systematically analyzes specific architectural elements of the Sagrada Família, attributing both biomimetic functions and biophilic qualities to each, supported by qualitative observations and references. The paper concludes by summarizing these findings and advocating for this combined approach in contemporary sustainable design.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: By integrating both the functional (biomimicry) and aesthetic/psychological (biophilia) principles derived from nature, architecture can achieve a more holistic and effective design. Biomimicry provides efficiency, strength, and resource conservation by mimicking nature's evolved systems. Biophilia satisfies innate human needs for nature connection, leading to well-being and restoration. When biomimetic functions are expressed through biophilic morphology, the resulting architecture is not only structurally sound and environmentally performant but also visually pleasing, psychologically restorative, and deeply resonant with human evolutionary preferences, creating a synergistic 'stronger wholeness' that goes 'beyond sustainability' to 'design for well-being'.

findings.antecedent: Equilibrated block system structure (mimicking trees' self-balancing growth)
findings.consequent: Structural stability, reduced material requirement, elimination of buttresses, open views, unique architectural forest, sense of refuge, biodiversity (variety of shapes/sizes), sensory variability (light), playfulness, enticement
findings.mechanism: By designing the structure to self-balance like individual trees, Gaudí eliminated external buttresses, leading to material efficiency and an open interior. The resulting varied forms and light play create a visually rich, protective, and engaging environment that resonates with human biophilic needs.
findings.quote: Gaudí's completely original idea was to base the structural design in considerations of equilibrium as in natural plants.

findings.antecedent: Tree-like branching columns (double-twisting, varying cross-sections, increasing sides with height, fractal patterns)
findings.consequent: Load transfer to floor, support roof, increased resistance, greater load bearing, reduced loads, extra lighting, soaring height, canopy-like effect, tessellation of sunflowers, varying columns, complexity and details, hierarchy, self-similarity
findings.mechanism: Mimicking tree growth and branching allows for efficient load distribution, enabling large windows and reducing wall load. The organic forms, varying geometry, and fractal patterns evoke a natural forest, providing a sense of refuge, visual enticement, and connection to nature.
findings.quote: The slender, fluted pillars slant gracefully toward each other before branching upward.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Giordano et al. (2013), Gómez et al. (2008), Lorenzi and Francaviglia (2010), Joshy (2018)

findings.antecedent: Catenary arches (mimicking human ribs/ribcage, reed-like visual expression)
findings.consequent: Transfer transverse loads, structural stability, reduced material, natural appearance, vegetation element hint, increased sense of stone-forest (refuge), originality, playfulness
findings.mechanism: Catenary forms naturally distribute loads as pure compression, eliminating horizontal thrust and buttresses, thus saving material. Their organic, reed-like appearance connects to nature, enhancing refuge and aesthetic pleasure by evoking natural forms.
findings.quote: Gaudí's catenary arches' visual expression was like that of reed, with a small hint to the connection of the ribcage at the top of some of the cloisters' vaults

findings.antecedent: Nonrectilinear geometry, ruled surfaces (paraboloids, hyperboloids), warped surfaces (ellipsoids, helicoids), fractal geometry (self-similarity, hierarchical patterns)
findings.consequent: Strongest, lightest, most efficient structures, thinner/finer structures, smooth connections, enhanced interior acoustics, better light capture/diffusion, reflecting/defusing surfaces, variability in color/light/textures, complexity/richness of details, enticement, self-similarity, hierarchy, visual comfort
findings.mechanism: Mimicking natural geometries (found in bones, plants, crystals) provides inherent structural strength and material efficiency, and improved acoustics. These complex, non-linear forms also create dynamic visual experiences and modulate light, satisfying biophilic needs for complexity, variability, and enticement.
findings.quote: He understood that Nature is constructed by laws of mathematics. What is strongest is inherently lightest and most efficient, and therefore most beautiful
findings.empirical_support_cited: Peach (2017), Cohn (2012), Collins (1963), Lorenzi and Francaviglia (2010), Gómez et al. (2008), Tomlow (2004), Tingley (2014), Lal (2015)

findings.antecedent: Inverted scale model (cords and pellets, mimicking cobwebs/catenaries)
findings.consequent: Precise and exact structural lines (compression only), no calculation needed, no possibility of error, sustainable structural elements, biophilic structural elements
findings.mechanism: By physically modeling the forces of tension in a suspended system and inverting it, Gaudí could directly visualize the optimal compression-only forms for masonry, ensuring structural efficiency and stability without complex calculations. This tool facilitated the creation of both functionally sound and biophilically expressive forms.
findings.quote: the exact shape of the church's structure was obtained by turning them upside-down, where the lines of tension formed by the ropes and weights would eventually indicate the pressure lines of the structure envisaged absolutely precise and exact, without having to conduct calculation and without possibility of error

findings.antecedent: Modular system (base measurement 7.5m, proportional divisions based on 12, referencing Montjuïc Hill height)
findings.consequent: Order and regulation of shapes/forms, repeated elements for molds, speed up work, fractal patterns, enticement, complexity, richness of details, universal scaling, sense of refuge, bringing building down to human scale, hierarchy
findings.mechanism: A consistent modular system, inspired by natural proportions and local context (Montjuïc Hill), ensures coherence and order throughout the design. This facilitates construction (molds) and creates fractal patterns that are visually engaging and provide a sense of scale and refuge, connecting the building to its environment and human perception.
findings.quote: all dimensions are governed by a modular system, which has a base measurement of 7.5 m

findings.antecedent: Ceramic mosaics from waste pieces (mimicking lizard skin)
findings.consequent: Protection for surfaces, reuse of materials, waste reduction, easier tile matching, minimum discards, flexible choices, reflecting surfaces, livability, movement, variability in colors/textures, richness of details, enticement
findings.mechanism: Inspired by lizard skin, this technique reuses waste ceramic, providing surface protection and reducing material consumption. The varied, reflective, and colorful mosaic surfaces create dynamic visual interest, contributing to livability, sensory variability, and enticement.
findings.quote: Gaudí invented a sustainable biomimetic technique (now called Trencadis) for designing ceramic mosaics from waste pieces

findings.antecedent: Bell towers with abat-sons (louvers), wind-catchers, self-shading device, corn ear/wheat spike forms, spiral stairs, bridges between towers
findings.consequent: Better acoustical performance (bell diffusion, sound travel with wind), passive ventilation (stack effect, cooler air), integrated self-shading, reduced heat gain/glare, daylight/warmth in cooler months, reflecting surfaces, foliage patterns, bridge complexity, hierarchy, self-similarity, air movement, livability, biodiversity, playfulness, enticement, prospect, refuge
findings.mechanism: Mimicking termite mounds for ventilation and using louvers for sound diffusion optimizes acoustic and thermal performance. The organic forms, fractal patterns, and connecting bridges create a visually rich, dynamic, and protective environment that satisfies biophilic needs for complexity, prospect, refuge, and playfulness.
findings.quote: the upper sections of the belfries have numerous openings with characteristic louvers (abat-sons) in all directions that will allow blind diffusion of bells' sound all over the neighborhood
findings.empirical_support_cited: Joshy (2018), Yoshikawa and Narita (2004), Everest and Pohlmann (2001), El Mahdi (2008)

findings.antecedent: Covered passages around basilica (mimicking Ploceidae nests), wide openings, Tree of Life pórtico, alabaster doves/pelican decoration
findings.consequent: Noise reduction, space for processions, natural illumination, wide openings (prospect), enclosure/shelter (refuge), biodiversity (vegetation/birds), sensory variability (air movement, light), fractal patterns, enticement, openness of views, access to multiple spaces
findings.mechanism: Inspired by weaver bird nests, the cloisters provide sheltered, enclosed spaces that reduce external noise while maintaining natural light and views. The organic forms, decorative elements (birds, Tree of Life), and fractal patterns create a restorative and engaging environment that fulfills biophilic needs for prospect, refuge, biodiversity, and sensory variability.
findings.quote: Gaudí's design of the cloisters in the Sagrada Família is like a Ploceidae nest surrounding the basilica

findings.antecedent: Stained-glass windows (transparent top, deeper hues below, cold colors east, warm colors west), dappled-leaves-like ceiling, hyperboloids with gold/green glass/tiles, lamps (mollusk shells, star-like), six lanterns for central altar
findings.consequent: High illumination in upper part (prospect), forest-like lighting effect (refuge), introspective atmosphere, light diffusion/reflection, rainbows of light, accentuation of verticality, livability, movement, sensory variability, playfulness, enticement, fractal effect
findings.mechanism: Mimicking natural light filtering through a forest canopy, Gaudí used varied stained-glass colors, light-diffusing surfaces, and strategically placed artificial lights to create dynamic and restorative lighting. This system provides both high illumination and a sense of refuge, while the varied colors and fractal patterns enhance sensory variability and aesthetic pleasure.
findings.quote: the glass is transparent on top to ensure high illumination for the church in the upper part (prospect), while deeper hues work their way down to create a forest-like lighting effect (refuge)

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Buildings designed with a combined biomimicry-biophilia approach will demonstrate superior structural efficiency, material conservation, and environmental performance (e.g., acoustics, lighting, ventilation) compared to designs focusing solely on one aspect or conventional designs.

Occupants of buildings designed with a combined biomimicry-biophilia approach will report higher levels of psychological well-being, aesthetic preference, and cognitive restoration compared to occupants of buildings designed with conventional or single-focus approaches.

The integration of fractal patterns, natural geometries, and varied sensory elements (light, texture, color) in architectural design will lead to increased visual comfort, reduced cognitive load, and enhanced feelings of enticement and playfulness.
The applicability of the biomimicry-biophilia approach should be tested in future studies.
The possibility to develop models from this design, and other comparable designs, into dynamic responsive systems is more conceivable.
Being applied, this will offer models and designs that are more satisfactory in terms of functional, environmental, and sustainable design, as well as humans' preference and psychological well-being.
bridge_warrants: The paper explicitly bridges biomimicry (functional, performance-based) and biophilia (aesthetic, psychological, human-centric) to create a more holistic design approach.
It connects historical architectural genius (Gaudí) with contemporary sustainable design challenges, suggesting historical precedents as valid reference models.
It links 'technical schemes' with 'biophilic settings' to enable the 'performance of nature into biophilic designs', advocating for a synergistic integration.
It suggests that 'new technologies, such as sensors, 3D printers, and developing software' can 'translate' Gaudí's design principles into 'contemporary modernized applications'.
methodological_critiques: Existing biomimicry research often results in designs that are not inherently sustainable and are visually poorly integrated into nature.
An exclusive focus on biophilic principles, without addressing ecological issues, does not guarantee better performance or higher well-being.

Modernist architecture's failure to meet human longing for beauty and details, and its deeming of 'superfluous elements' (later found to trigger positive neurophysiology), represents a mistake contemporary biomimetic architects risk repeating by neglecting aesthetics, patterns, and compositions.

The concern that historical models relied on obsolete knowledge and tools is addressed, but the paper acknowledges this as a general critique, though not valid for Sagrada Família due to its ongoing contemporary completion.
model_structure: The paper proposes a conceptual model where architectural design integrates three levels of biomimicry (organism, behavior, ecosystem) and their five dimensions (form, material, construction, process, function) with the biophilic qualities defined by Kellert-Heerwagen (prospect, refuge, livability/movement, biodiversity, sensory variability, fractals, playfulness, enticement). The Sagrada Família serves as a 'reference model' or 'platform' for this integrated approach, implying a synergistic relationship where functional biomimetic solutions are expressed through biophilic forms, leading to enhanced sustainability, efficiency, and human well-being.
limitations: The study presents only one example (Sagrada Família), and further models need to be developed by creative minds.
The applicability of the biomimicry-biophilia approach needs to be tested in future empirical studies.
Gaudí's original design intent for Sagrada Família likely did not include reducing resource consumption, implying sustainability was a consequence rather than an explicit goal.

mechanism_chain.description: Gaudí's biomimetic structural design (equilibrated block system) leads to architectural features that evoke natural environments, thereby promoting well-being through biophilic responses.
